lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.unitTitle: Job Readiness: Applications, Resumes, and Interviews
lessonRef.title: Guided practice: gathering references appropriately

objective: Learners identify two people outside their family who could genuinely speak to their reliability or work, and draft the message they would send to ask permission to list each as a reference, without sending it, so they understand what makes an appropriate reference and how to ask respectfully.
scenario: The learner names two non-family adults who know their work directly (such as a teacher, coach, club leader, or volunteer supervisor), explains in one sentence what each could honestly speak to, and drafts (but does not send) a short, polite message asking permission to list them as a reference.
safetyNotes: This draft is never sent as part of the lesson; no real message is required to reach anyone.
A reference should be someone who has directly observed the learner's work, not simply someone who likes them; the task requires naming what each person could honestly speak to.
materials: the four-part permission-request pattern on this task sheet

tasks.directions: List two non-family adults who have directly observed your work, and one sentence on what each could honestly speak to.

prompts.text: Name two people and, for each, one honest thing they could speak to based on what they've actually seen you do.

tasks.directions: Draft a short, polite permission-request message for one of the two people, asking before listing them as a reference.

prompts.text: My draft asks permission before assuming the person agrees to be a reference.
My draft gives enough context (what I'm applying for, and roughly when they might be contacted) that the person can decide.

tasks.directions: Explain why each of your two chosen people is an appropriate reference and not just someone who likes you.

prompts.text: For each of your two people, explain what they have directly observed that makes them able to honestly speak to your work, not just a friendly relationship.

tasks.directions: Reflect on what makes a reference request respectful.

prompts.text: Name one thing your draft message does to make it easy for the person to say no if they're not comfortable, and why that matters.

remediation: If a learner names someone who only knows them socially with nothing to observe about their work, reteach by contrasting 'knows me' with 'has seen me do something specific' using two side-by-side examples, then have the learner reconsider their two choices against that distinction.
extension: Have the learner draft a second permission-request message for a person in a different context (for example, a coach instead of a teacher) and compare what details changed between the two messages.
